newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: S.Pacific nations to cut tariffs to reform economi.
newsitem.headline: S.Pacific nations to cut tariffs to reform economi.

text.p: Leading South Pacific nations on Friday agreed to slash tariffs, increase budget transparency and implement sweeping reforms to boost economic growth and reduce aid dependence.

Economic ministers from the 16-member South Pacific forum agreed at their inaugural summit to adopt an action plan and work towards free trade in the region extending from Australia to the Cook Islands.
"Our goal is free and open trade and investment, the summit's host, Australian Treasurer Peter Costello told reporters in this tropical Australian resort town.
"It's a pretty ambitious declaration that we've put in the action plan."
The group includes Australia and New Zealand and 14 Pacific island nations, including Papua New Guinea and Fiji.
Friday's agreement put no timetable on implementing reforms, noting only that the pace and make-up of reforms would be "appropriate to our individual circumstances".

The action plan reforms also include boosting private sector development, improve regulatory and transparency measures, liberalise investment policies and reduce government spending and public sectors.
The forum's two largest members, Australia and New Zealand, have economies that dwarf those of other members.
Foreign aid, particularly from Canberra, Wellington and Washington, plays a key role in supporting living standards.

The remaining 14 members -- all island countries with small populations -- are the Cook Islands, Fiji, Kiribati, the Marshall Islands, the Federated States of Micronesia, Nauru, Niue, Papua New Guinea, Palau, Samoa, the Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu and Vanuatu.
They have economies marked by low growth, surging imports, high debt, bloated public sectors and weak private sectors, and foreign aid accounting for up to 70 percent of their gross domestic product.
Exports are largely resources, fishing rights and tourism.

Some have begun basic economic reforms, but forum leaders acknowledged at their last summit, in September, 1996, that they needed to speed the pace of change to boost their economic strength and encourage foreign investment.
